title: The Philadelphia Experiment
short: A secret Navy experiment where a ship allegedly became invisible and teleported.

content.text: According to conspiracy theories, in 1943 the USS Eldridge was subject to a secret experiment in Philadelphia, becoming cloaked in green fog and disappearing.
Witnesses claim the ship reappeared 300 km away, and parts of the crew allegedly became fused with the ship's metal.
The myth was popularized by Morris Jessup in 1955, after he received letters from a man named Carl Allen (also known as Carlos Allende), who claimed to have seen it.
Carl Allen said he saw the ship disappear. He later sent heavily annotated copies of Jessup’s book, suggesting there was a deeper conspiracy.
Skeptics found that Allen was not a reliable witness – his stories were full of contradictions, and many consider him a fantasist.
Some explanations: the U.S. Navy tested ‘degaussing’ (demagnetizing) technology on warships in that era, which may explain claims of green fog and disappearance.
Another project, called ‘Project Mogul’, might explain wreckage: it used radar balloon arrays, which could have been mistaken for UFO debris.
In summary: no concrete proof of teleportation or invisibility. The story persists because of its mystery, but most evidence points to a mixture of misunderstanding, hoaxes, and real military tech.

title: Roswell Alien Autopsy
short: Claims of bodies and film from a 1947 UFO crash in New Mexico.

content.text: The Roswell incident in July 1947 is one of the most famous UFO stories: an alleged alien spacecraft crashed near Roswell, New Mexico.
Eyewitnesses and conspiracy theorists claim that bodies of extraterrestrials were recovered and kept secret by the U.S. government.
In 1995, British producer Ray Santilli released footage of an alien autopsy, saying the film was real.
Skeptics later pointed out that the creature in the film resembles props made by sculptor John Humphreys, who worked on sci-fi movies.
Santilli claimed he made a re-enactment because the original film deteriorated — but many believe the whole thing was a hoax to make money.
Investigations revealed that a famous ‘alien corpse’ photo might actually show a two-year-old child’s body preserved earlier, not an alien.
Moreover, leaked documents reference U.S. projects like ‘High Dive’ (parachute system testing) and ‘Mogul’ (balloon surveillance), which may explain wreckage and observed anomalies.
Conclusion: No scientifically verifiable alien bodies. While Roswell remains a cultural touchstone for UFO believers, the strongest evidence points to misidentification, propaganda, and hoaxes.

title: Area 51
short: A highly classified U.S. military base surrounded by rumors about UFOs, aliens, and underground complexes.

content.text: Area 51 became legendary thanks to rumors that the government studies alien technology there, hides crashed UFOs, and conducts secret experiments.
The base is located in Nevada. Google Maps shows it, but Street View refuses to load nearby roads. For years, the Pentagon denied its existence.
Facts show the base tests advanced aircraft like the F-117 Nighthawk. A secret terminal in Las Vegas flies employees directly to Area 51, operated by NASA.
The base became widely known after the Roswell incident, when supposed alien bodies were allegedly transported here, inspiring claims of autopsies.
The perimeter has warning signs, mines, thermal cameras, microphones, and armed private contractors who patrol in white trucks.
Intruders are usually arrested rather than shot, but the consequences can be serious.
Some theories say the base has a massive underground multi-level complex connected by tunnels, similar to the Hive in 'Resident Evil'.
Others claim world leaders meet with extraterrestrial civilizations inside Area 51.
Some 'former scientists' claim they dissected aliens, but there is no real proof.
The truth will remain hidden until the government decides to talk — which is unlikely.

title: The Loch Ness Monster
short: A legendary creature said to inhabit Loch Ness in Scotland — from ancient sightings to modern sonar scans.

content.text: The legend tells of a giant creature living in Scotland’s Loch Ness, known as the Loch Ness Monster — or Nessie. Some describe it as a plesiosaur-like reptile with diamond-shaped fins.
The earliest known mention comes from Roman legionaries, who carved strange beasts they saw in Scotland — including a creature resembling Nessie.
A later written account appears in the biography of St. Columba, an Irish monk. He supposedly witnessed the creature attacking a girl in the lake, and drove it away with a prayer.
In 1934, London doctor Kenneth Wilson published the most famous 'photo' of Nessie. The world believed it — until his partners later exposed it as a hoax.
However, sonar research showed massive moving objects deep in the lake, able to rise and swim independently. What they are remains unknown.

In 2007, researcher Gordon Holmes placed microphones in the lake and filmed a 15-meter creature moving at 10 km/h. Experts confirmed the footage was real, but some scientists argued it could have been an unusually large insect or worm.
Even Google Earth once showed something mysterious in the lake — but it turned out to be a boat shadow.
Skeptics say the lake’s biomass is too small to support a giant predator and its family. They also note that Scotland was once covered by ice, and no known animal could survive such conditions.
Believers claim Nessie swims in and out of the lake through hidden underwater tunnels connecting to the sea.
Tourism in the area thrives thanks to the legend, and many hope Nessie is real — even without proof.
A curious theory suggests creatures like Nessie or Bigfoot may appear through temporary rifts in time, explaining why they show up and vanish.

title: The Yeti and Bigfoot
short: A mysterious humanoid creature reported around the world — from the Himalayas to America.

content.text: In 1921, an expedition climbing Everest heard terrifying screams behind a hill. When they went to investigate, they found huge human-like footprints. Europeans started calling the creature the 'Abominable Snowman'.
In 1951, explorer Eric Shipton photographed giant barefoot tracks on Everest — a 31×16 cm footprint. The USSR even formed a commission dedicated to catching Bigfoot.
Different cultures have different names for this creature: in Tibet it’s Yeti, in America it’s Bigfoot or Sasquatch (meaning 'wild man'), and in Siberia some joke that it’s the 'Wandering Chukcha'.
According to witnesses, animals behave strangely when Yeti appears: birds scatter, beasts run away, and humans feel panic.
The word 'panic' supposedly comes from the Greek god Pan — a hairy nature spirit who terrified those who saw him, and whose image later influenced the concept of the snowman.
People claim that Yeti cannot be photographed clearly because he can 'overexpose film' or disrupt electronics.
In 1967, two Americans filmed a famous video of a 'walking Bigfoot', but in 2002 their relatives admitted it was a man in a costume.
In 2013, geneticist Bryan Sykes analyzed two hair samples from the Himalayas. DNA showed they belonged to an ancient polar bear species that lived over 40,000 years ago.
Some believe there are different types of these creatures: mountain Yetis living in caves, forest ones building tree shelters, and — jokingly — the 'Couch Yeti'.
Ancient depictions of snowman-like creatures were found in Greece, Armenia, Rome, and elsewhere, suggesting the myth is very old.
Biologists argue that for a species to survive, at least 100 individuals must exist — yet none have been definitively documented.
A standing bear can easily be mistaken for a huge humanoid, reaching up to 5 meters when upright.
The Yeti has reportedly been seen everywhere except the North Pole. In one region of Russia, the governor even offered a million rubles for capturing one.
Some theories suggest Yetis are an alternate evolutionary branch of humans — more psychophysical than social — and that their presence causes headaches, panic, and even tumors.
A more dramatic theory claims these beings may survive if humanity destroys itself, acting as a 'backup version' of Homo sapiens.
There is no solid evidence that the Yeti or Bigfoot truly exists. But eyewitnesses insist they saw something — and maybe their stories aren’t pure insanity after all.

title: Men in Black
short: Mysterious figures often linked to conspiracy theories and alien abductions, who show up unexpectedly and act like federal agents investigating what you’ve seen.

content.text: Men in Black frequently appear in mass culture and conspiracy theories related to UFOs and alien abductions. They often show up at people’s homes, claiming to be federal agents trying to find out what witnesses have seen.

The term was first introduced by American writers Gray Barker and John Kelley in 1967. Barker attributed them significant influence on world history, claiming they had encounters with figures like Caesar, Napoleon, and Jefferson.
These men are said to appear and disappear mysteriously. One witness described chasing black Cadillacs that vanished suddenly when cornered.
There’s a website called 'theyknewtoomuch.com' dedicated to Gray Barker's work, and ironically, a movie is being made based on his books.
The earliest reported sighting dates back to 1880, when a couple found strange objects, only to be approached later by a man in black claiming to be a collector who bought their find.
In 1953, Albert Bender created a UFO organization but was ordered to disband it by mysterious men in black Cadillacs dressed in all black, except their white shirts and red ties.
These men operate outside official law enforcement or government, caring little about laws. Their visits are unapproved and often intimidating.
Agents Mulder and Scully from 'The X-Files' are basically fictional Men in Black, traveling the world investigating strange phenomena while bending laws and suppressing others with similar abilities.
Some theories say Men in Black aren't even human but electromagnetic intelligences capable of emitting different frequencies and taking any form, even your harmless cat.
In 2008, a viral video surfaced allegedly showing Men in Black in an Israeli hotel. Witnesses described them as tall, identical-looking men wearing black suits and dark glasses.

There’s a cosmic war theory claiming 30,000 years ago humans fought dragon gods, who after winning, became the reptilian aliens known as Men in Black. They supposedly interfere with all major events, suppressing discovery and innovation.
Some say these beings can appear terrifyingly robotic or lizard-like, and conspiracy fans link them to secret government operatives or alien overlords controlling human society.
Skeptics dismiss it all as nonsense, but believers swear they’ve seen something unexplainable.

title: Stonehenge
short: A mysterious stone monument in England, surrounded by countless theories — from aliens to ancient calendars — but its true purpose remains unclear.

content.text: Stonehenge is a complex of stone structures located in Wiltshire, England. It is one of the most famous archaeological sites and a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
Despite being almost ruined, Stonehenge still holds many mysteries with no definite answers. Theories about its origin range from Atlanteans and aliens to druids and even nuclear reactors.
No one knows the exact year it was built or who exactly constructed it. The remaining structure looks different from how it originally was.
Some conspiracy theories claim it’s a cosmic launch pad or a portal to another world, but these are often spread by fanatics and are not supported by evidence.
In 1954, some people started to believe that Stonehenge was actually built then, fueled by fake photos circulating online showing cranes and concrete being used.
However, this was just restoration work, not original construction. Restoration at Stonehenge began as early as 1901, with stones being raised and stabilized to prevent collapse.
The 1954 restoration involved repositioning stones, concrete reinforcement, and even moving some stones. Some stones today are replicas, not originals.
Dr. Christopher Chippindale, chief curator at the Archaeology Museum, confirms that most stones were moved and reinforced during restorations.
Skeptics claim that historical engravings and documents, such as the 1440 woodcut and the 1668 Frederick VI map, also prove Stonehenge existed long before the modern restorations.
Stonehenge might not be unique; similar ancient stone structures exist, suggesting it was part of a broader tradition of megalithic construction.

The most accepted theory is that Stonehenge functioned as an ancient calendar, used to track the sun’s solstices and possibly lunar cycles and eclipses — an early computational technology without robots.
The site predates the druids, who later used it for rituals, but they were not its original builders.
Visitors today can explore Stonehenge but must keep a distance of about 15 meters, with close access reserved only for those following druidic traditions.
Critical thinking is important when approaching theories about Stonehenge — separate facts from myths and don't fall for conspiracy traps.
